Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. in view of yesterday's admission by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) to the House of Commons finance committee that his government's policy of raising interest rates almost in lock-step with United States rates will have depressive effects on the Canadian economy, in view of the fact that this interest rate policy will impose additional costs on Canadian taxpayers, for example because of the higher Canada Savings Bond rates which will have to be paid, and the necessity for substantially greater unemployment insurance and welfare payments, and in view of the Conservative government's promise to bring more openness to the budget-making process, and in particular to make financial forecasts and estimates available to the public, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand):
That this House order the Minister of Finance to issue a directive to the governor of the Bank of Canada to provide to the House the results, in detail, of the Bank of Canada's analysis of the effects of the increases in interest rates since May 22, 1979, on jobs, economic growth, housing and food costs and the number of consumer and small business bankruptcies over the coming year.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Labour. Yesterday in answer to a very serious question from the hon. member for Louis-Hebert he said that unfortunately, when it comes to labour relations, the dismissal or lay-off of workers or the loss of jobs by workers is like a death penalty. I want to ask him whether he is willing to support the recommendations of the Cossette report which was released to both parties and particularly whether he is willing to intervene personally to find an amicable arrangement between both parties.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lincoln M. Alexander (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT IS READY TO SUPPORT RECOMMENDATIONS OF COSSETTE REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member wants to get involved in this matter: I commend him for it. However, he must appreciate that the inquiry was called for by the Maritime Employers' Association as well as the International Longshoremen's Association, two locals. It was at their request that Labour Canada brought forward this inquiry.
As I indicated earlier, the report was released to the parties affected and, of course, all we can do at this time is to sit back and wait until we hear from the parties. It is not my role now to indicate to the parties what they should do; they are the ones who asked for the report; they are the ones who asked for the inquiry in order to determine what was going to happen with longshoremen and checkers as a result of the very hazy and uncertain position, in terms of employment, in the future. FINANCE, TRADE AND ECONOMIC AFFAIRS CONCURRENCE IN FIRST REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
that the first report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, presented to the House on Wednesday, October 24, 1979, be concurred in.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the motion for concurrence before the House today refers to the first report of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. The report was tabled in the House on October 24 by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) who is chairman of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
I should like to read the substance of that report.
Your Committee met on Tuesday, October 23, 1979, and agreed to express its dismay that none of the ministers or officials of the departments and agencies whose estimates were referred to this committee were able to appear before the committee at eight o'clock p.m., Tuesday, October 23 and recommends that the Flouse formally remind all ministers and their officials that they are primarily servants of Parliament and owe Parliament and its committees their priority attention in view especially of the commitment of the new government to give a greater role to Parliament and its committees.
That motion was proposed to the committee by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), and it was proposed because of the difficulty which had been experienced by members of the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in finding ministers or departmental officials who were prepared to appear before the committee on that particular evening, Tuesday, October 23.
I should say that the subcommittee had authorized the clerk to contact the various ministries, and I should name the ministers who were contacted. 1 might say also that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs is probably one of the busiest standing committees; there is always a tremendous amount of legislation before it in addition to the estimates of three departments-Finance, Trade and Commerce, and National Revenue.
When it was found impossible to have the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) appear before the committee-hon. members will recall his stating in this House that he was not prepared to appear before the committee until after the committee had seen and questioned the governor of the Bank of Canada-the committee members looked for an alternative, bearing in mind that they had to study the estimates of three different ministries.

Committee Report
The alternatives were the minister who sits in the other place, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. de Cotret), or, if he could not attend, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry (Mr. Huntington), or, if he could not attend, the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Wilson), or, if he could not attend, the President of the Privy Council and Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Baker). There were four ministers, if the Minister of Finance was going to continue to refuse to appear that evening, or, as the motion reads, the departmental officials of those departments.
As an individual I find it astonishing and most regrettable that in a committee which is so busy, a committee which wanted to continue to discuss very important topics, the government was not prepared so to organize itself that one of the responsible ministers could attend. 1 want to point a finger particularly at the Minister of National Revenue because he is also the leader of the government side in this House. It fell on his shoulders, therefore, to ensure that at least one of the ministers was available to appear before the committee.
In my opinion the motion is one of censure on the government for its failure to ensure that the committee was in a position to do its job. I sincerely regret that, because of the lack of time available to one of the most important committees of this House, we were unable to question the minister responsible for industry, trade and commerce or the two ministers of state allied with that ministry. This motion for concurrence has been brought before the House in order to emphasize the point that in difficult times such as we are facing today, when it is so important to question ministers on their new policies, it is most regrettable it should have been found impossible for any one of four ministers or any officials of the ministries represented by those ministers to appear before the committee. Regretfully, therefore, I bring before the House this motion for concurrence.

As his counterpart in the New Democratic Party I do not have the opportunity to ask that minister any questions with respect to government policy.
I might point out that in addition to his other responsibilities he is chairman of the economic committee of the inner cabinet and therefore the most influential member of the cabinet with respect to economic policy. In these circumstances it is extraordinary he should not be in this House. In fact I would be happy to resign my seat if he cares to come to Broadview-Greenwood and face the electorate in an election.

It is up to him to decide whether he wishes to do so. I say that in all sincerity. Since he is not in this House he has an even greater obligation to all members of the committee, regardless of party, to make his time available to the committee and to appear in the very limited period we have in which to do our work.
I join with the hon. member for Vaudreuil in expressing my concern, and bring once again to the attention of the House the fact that the chief economic adviser to the Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) is not a member of this chamber, the difficulty in which this places members of the opposition and, in particular, members of this party which does not have any representation in the Senate.
It is high time the chief economic adviser to the government was a member of this House. The least he could do would be to make himself available when a committee is meeting and when it has a very tight schedule before it because of the workload it is carrying. He should at least have the courtesy to appear before it. We are moving in ways which are an affront not only to the committee but to democracy itself, and it is worth taking a little time to draw attention to this aspect and, once again, to underline the absurdity of the chief economic adviser to the cabinet not being a member of this House.
The present arrangement constitutes an affront to members of the House of Commons and places members of this party, in particular, in a difficult position because they are not in a position to question him to find out what his policies are, how he feels about the interest rate, how he feels about the effects on trade and development, how he feels about industrial strategy, and how he feels about the general direction the government is taking. It is ludicrous that this gentleman is not a member of this House and that he is not presenting himself for election in the by-elections which are being held. In all sincerity I offer, if he wants to come down to Broadview-Greenwood and contest that seat, I will gladly resign, contest it, and take him on.

Mr. Chairman, this clause was designed to prevent the artificial creation of capital losses. Section 85(4) of the act stipulates that no capital loss is recognized where a taxpayer disposes of a property to a corporation which he controls. If the taxpayer owns shares of the corporation acquiring the property, the disallowed loss is added to the cost of his shares and will serve to reduce any capital gain on their ultimate disposal. Where the taxpayer does not own any shares of the corporation, the disallowed loss is added to the cost of the property to the purchaser corporation. In effect, the property in these circumstances is rolled over, that is, its cost to the corporation is equal to its cost in the hands of the taxpayer prior to the transaction. Subclause 14(1) is relieving and corrects a technical deficiency in the provision described.
Subclause 14(2) is a consequential change related to the changes to subsection 13(7.1) of the act. This change provides uniform treatment for the investment tax credit claimed by a co-operative corporation for purposes of computing capital gains on the depreciable property.

Income Tax Act
This and the clause which follows are of interest to resource companies in the mining, oil and gas industries. Section 66 provides for the deduction of Canadian and foreign exploration and development expenses. Also the section defines a Canadian resource property, principal business corporation and shareholder corporation of a joint exploration company. This clause makes a number of amendments to section 66 of the act.
In the first place it introduces a requirement for joint elections where Canadian exploration and development expenses incurred after 1971 and before May 7, 1974, by one company called a predecessor corporation are transferred or carried over for deduction by another corporation, a successor corporation or a second successor corporation. This election is designed to avoid disputes which have arisen in the past between taxpayers as to whether these so-called succcessor corporation rules are to apply. The election ensures that both the transferor and transferee agree that these special rules are intended to apply. A similar change is proposed for the transfer of Canadian exploration expense in section 66.1 of the act and Canadian development expense in section 66.2. As I understand that, it is to ensure that two people are not claiming the same deduction for expenses.
The second change in section 66 extends the deduction with respect to the exploration and development expenses of a successor corporation. These expenses are deducted only against the income of the successor corporation from the properties transferred to it from a predecessor corporation. The change will permit these expenses to be deducted from certain reserves transferred by a predecessor corporation which arose in connection with the sale of resource property.
There are two more provisions. A third change to this section of the act will clarify that the right to store petroleum, natural gas or other related hydrocarbons is a "Canadian resource property" as defined. This change ensures that both the vendor and the purchaser of a resource property receive similar tax treatment. An amendment to Bill C-37 clarifies that this rule only applies to underground storage rights. I believe Bill C-37 was introduced after the budget of the previous Parliament. The purchaser will include the cost in his cumulative Canadian development expense, and the vendor will deduct the proceeds from the balance of his unclaimed Canadian development expense.
The final change to section 66 is to remove the references to syndicates or associations in the definition of foreign exploration and development expenses, etc. Under our tax law there is no tax status for a syndicate or association. Therefore these words are rather irrelevant.

This takes us into the area which I thought we would get into. Certainly we will get into that area by the time we reach consideration of clause 20. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member has just pointed out, the principal effect of this clause is to extend the date of the 100 per cent write-off provision for Canadian exploration expenses for individual and non-principal business corporations. That provision originally applied until June 30 of this year. It was extended by the previous minister of finance by a remission order to the end of this calendar year. The provision would be extended by this bill to December 31, 1981.
The effect is to permit a 100 per cent write-off in the first year of those expenses. In that sense it is a tax deferral because what is written off in the first year cannot be written off in subsequent years. The effect, I am informed, in the first year is to postpone some $80 million of revenue.

The question one must ask is, deferred until when? The parliamentary secretary knows that these things are accumulative and are continually deferred as time goes on. Therefore, there is no reckoning day that one could predict. What will happen is that it will continue to be deferred as exploration continues.
There is a very basic question here, and it relates to the question of oil prices, the question of the relationship between our manufacturing sector and our resource sector, to the survival of PetroCan, to the fact that we have subsidized-not only through this particular measure, but through other measures-the drilling allowance, and to the special shelters that have been created for wealthy investors in the frontier allowance field, all these expenditures. I am delighted that the Minister of Finance will be indicating what these expenditures are. I hope those expenditures will include deferrals because they, too, are a form of expenditure.
But all of these measures, the fast write-offs, the super depreciation, depletion and so on, are a form of public expenditure which subsidizes some forms of economic activity at the expense of others, and in which the government and the taxpayers are subsidizing particular companies and particular concerns. I think that it is worth while to point out to the government that the effective rate of taxation of the five large petroleum companies between 1974 and 1978 was 17.9 per cent and that the effective rate of taxation of medium-sized companies, including Dome Petroleum which does not pay any taxes, was 17.7 per cent.
The member for Saint-Henri-Westmount says that one cannot compare a company to an ordinary individual, that a corporation cannot be dealt with as though it were a person, but that we must recognize when talking about a corporation that we are talking about shareholders, investors, and that
Income Tax Act
therefore we must relate it to the individual tax system. That is well and fine, but 1 would simply point out that the average income of those people who are investing in the companies with which we are concerned is far higher than the average or medium income in Canada.
We also have to recognize that this interference, and this is one more example of it, with the operation of the so-called free market in which members opposite are so proud to be believers, creates tremendous distortions.
It might be worth while if I quote what Professor Bossons, an economist at the University of Toronto, said when asked for his views on current tax allowances in the energy field. His views were reported in The Globe and Mail for October 17, 1979. He said:
I certainly don't have the feeling that the incentives are inadequate. They're extremely generous.
As he sees it, these allowances have the effect of encouraging a trend toward concentration in the industry. I do not think he is a member of my party, but I want to read what he had to say. He said:
The companies that can take advantage are mainly the large vertically integrated ones.
Mr. Bossons contended that the incentives are aimed mainly at tapping profits rather than at influencing investment. He summed up the package of existing incentives as "a lot of second-best attempts to offset byproducts of other second-best attempts."
He also suggested that allowing oil companies to reduce their effective rate of taxation limits the ability of government to provide incentives for areas of the economy that could produce more jobs. And it tends to increase taxes in real terms in other industries while lowering them in the oil industry.
Government must make a conscious choice in devising incentives, so that it doesn't overstimulate one industry at the expense of another, Mr. Bossons said. One reason for formation of Petro-Canada, he suggested, was to attempt to get a little more competition in the oil industry. Without the Crown oil company Ottawa would be "essentially at the mercy of the industry that's not far away from being a cartel."
Mr. Bossons said foreign ownership of the oil industry is actually being encouraged by the current tax rules. If the system were neutral the incentives would be "things that can be taken advantage of exactly as easily by 'domestic' companies as by the foreign-owned concerns."
These are very critical questions. Obviously the parliamentary secretary is not in a position to answer them today. I want to suggest to the parliamentary secretary, and through him to the minister, that when it comes time for the budget and for a decision on oil prices, I want him to recognize that when we talk about the 1980s and the amount of capital resources to be expended on research and development in the oil and natural gas industry, unless this is done properly and fairly two or three things will happen, although they have been happening since the 1970s.
The parliamentary secretary may recall that it was Mr. Kierans who resigned from the Liberal cabinet precisely because in 1972 he could see the writing on the wall. He could see the dramatic distortions which would be taking place in the Canadian economy if we continued to give as we did give right through the 1970s the tremendous incentives and advantages to the oil industry, whereas no incentive or advantage was

October 31, 1979
Income Tax Act
given to the manufacturing or processing industry in Canada. As a result of that we have seen the dramatic weakening of our manufacturing base and the tragedy of an $11 billion deficit in the trade of finished goods that we have now. That is a direct result of incentive and tax policies by the Government of Canada which was initiated in the 1970s. That is one thing that will continue in the 1980s. But we will have a continued distortion and domination of our oil industry by foreign companies, subsidized by the Canadian taxpayer.
With the elimination of Petro-Canada, we are eliminating the only competition that exists in that vital industry as well as the only means we have at the moment of seeing precisely what is going on in the fields of exploration, research and development, and in other related energy fields. You cannot separate these questions. The Liberals failed to do so as we saw in the dramatic failure which occurred in the 1970s. That failure has led to an extraordinary subsidy amounting to billions of dollars to the oil industry at the expense of not just the principle of fairness-which I have spoken about earlier- but also the structure of Canadian industry and our ability to survive as an industrial nation. 1 think it is vital for the parliamentary secretary to take our concerns to the minister.
Let me say this as well, that one of the excuses which the oil industry has been using against the Canadian people for having these extraordinary-and they are extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination-subsidies of these vast multinational corporations by the taxpayer is that by keeping the price of oil down it forces us to rely on these fast write offs as a means of finding ways to finance the necessary research, development and exploration.
I have never been persuaded by that excuse. It is not borne out by the profit figures which they have been giving us. If that excuse is true, then there is one thing the Minister of Finance will be able to do in this budget provided that he has an agreement on oil pricing and a strategy for oil pricing in the 1980s.
No longer will the oil companies have the excuse of relying on a two-fold subsidy. But instead of having the one major subsidy we had in the 1970s, which subsidy was right through the tax system, in the 1980s they want an additional one. They want an addition to the tax subsidy. They want an extraordinary subsidy of price, if you like.
We are entitled to get from the parliamentary secretary- and if he cannot get it for us today I guess we will have to wait for the Conservative budget-an explanation from the minister as to the logic of this policy in terms of the relationship between the different sectors of the economy as to why we are allowing such extraordinary write-offs in one sector and not in another. I think we are also entitled from the point of view of a good deal for the Canadian people to ask ourselves why, when we are entering into an economy where the public corporation can apparently survive only with the incredible series of crutches and supports of incentives and grants of direct money and of tax expenditures from the Canadian public, we receive nothing in return?
[Mr. Rae.l
We are told by the provinces we have no right to the resources. We are told by the oil companies that we are interfering in the private enterprise system at the same time as this whole structure depends on an incredible number of incentives, grants, write-offs, and tax depreciations which result in a serious loss of taxation to the Canadian public.
I hope we will have a clear statement from the parliamentary secretary as to what he thinks the effective rate of taxation in those industries should be. If he thinks it should be down to 18, 17 or 16 per cent, then I hope the government will come clean and say that is the policy of the Government of Canada and that we expect the Canadian people to bear this price when the normal corporate rate is 46 per cent. I think the people of Canada are entitled to know what they are getting in exchange for this extraordinary expenditure.
Finally, if we move toward a world price, and we on this side of the House think that will be a disaster, and not necessary, but if the government insists on moving toward the world price-no doubt there would be no difference if the Liberal party were in power-we are then entitled to say to them, "Look, to pay one tribute is enough, and if the oil companies are determined to let the so-called world market in oil determine their price system, then do not come back to the public trough for the second time."
You cannot have the best of both worlds. You cannot move toward the world price and continue this absurd situation of subsidizing to such a great extent the takeover of our own resources and the development of our country. This tax question is profound. It relates to the industrial future. It relates to the future of the economic system and how much longer we can continue subsidizing these large corporations without having any say or influence in their policy, without having any policy to control the direction and investment, apart from using these various carrots that have been thrown in front of them since they went on strike in 1974.
We are entitled to put on the record how deep our concerns are, and how ill-advised the Liberal party was. It led to a foreign takeover of our resource industry. We are in a bad situation and the policies that are being continued by this government will only confirm our difficulties. This will confirm our status in the world as basically dependent on foreign multinational companies for the development of our own natural resources. It will confirm how our industrial structure is weakened because of this. The fairness of this tax break is also brought into question.
For all those reasons, Mr. Chairman, this measure is wrong and should be defeated. It has no place in the budget of a self-respecting people who are prepared to take the industrial and resource future into their own hands. We reject it out of hand as an approach. It is deplorable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member has detected a difference, a difference in climate and some of the slight modifications made to the original Bill C-37 that are embodied in the bill before us. The further steps he might reasonably anticipate will no doubt come in the budget, and some of the subsequent programs of the government will be designed to get the economy of the country moving again, as we all wish it to do.
May 1 comment on some of the points raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood. He strayed, perhaps consciously, a long way from the provisions of the clause before us. In fact some of his remarks might well be construed as support for what this clause does. He spoke of what he considers to be undue benefits to the oil companies. As I am sure he knows, this particular clause might be construed as a step to ensure that other potential and actual investors in exploration are on the same basis or on a not less favourable basis than an oil company. This extension of the right to charge exploration expenses in the year made, applies to individuals and non-principal business corporations, as the unwieldy phrase goes.
Some of the hon. member's comments in a more general vein do deserve a reaction. One of the tests of any incentive

October 31, 1979
Income Tax Act
given by way of taxes or otherwise in the market economy is whether it works. The incentive given here is really a deferral of taxes, a deferral which does not go on for ever. The first deferral is paid when there is income to tax it against and, if one looks at it logically, it is future exploration expenses which are deferred thereafter. So there may be a turn-over of deferred taxes if a company continues its exploration activities on a sufficient scale depending to some degree, of course, on the revenue eventually achieved.
I think it would be hard to say in the circumstances facing this country, that the amount of exploration for oil and gas here is excessive. Our concern is that it has not been greater. Some of the sources to which we now have to look for future reserves are, by and large, very expensive either because of exceptionally adverse weather conditions and distances involved, or because production costs are higher than we have been accustomed to. If the point is reached at which taxes on the industry and all kinds of investors in this search for energy becomes excessive, become obviously wasteful, only then will we be able to say that the tax arrangements are too attractive. That, I believe, is the test of any tax incentive or other kind of incentive given to an industry of any kind, not just to the oil industry.
The hon. member also attempted to suggest that the deterioration in manufacturing competitiveness in this country was due to the inducements given to mining and oil company exploration. 1 find that a farfetched explanation of an undoubted fact. There has, indeed, been a deterioration in the competitive position of manufacturing in this country and the situation has only been saved, and that temporarily, by the depreciation of the dollar, a depreciation which marks the failure, not the success, of economic policy.
1 doubt that the decline in the competitiveness of manufacturing industry in this country was in any way due to excessive direction of capital to mining and oil exploration activities. I believe there are much more evident and realistic causes therefor-one could look for them in levels of wages and salaries in this country which exceeded those in the United States at a time when our productivity was known to be, on average, 15 to 20 per cent lower than theirs. Whatever the causes of that situation, the effect on the declining competitiveness of Canadian manufacturing can be seen, whereas the effect the hon. member appeared to suggest cannot be seen.
I end by making two points. First, this particular clause is not addressed to the oil companies but to individuals and non-oil companies whose principal business is not in oil exploration. Its purpose is to induce investment from both sources, not, as the hon. member suggested, to add to monopoly or near cartel, as he chooses to call it, but rather the reverse-to get more people into the act. In the second place, the final test will be whether it provides the results intended. The evidence so far is that it has produced results and its extension is therefore more than warranted.

I do not want to delay the discussion, Mr. Chairman, but I believe there are definite examples which might change the mind of the hon. member from the

New Democratic Party who was speaking just a few minutes ago. I recall the time when members of the New Democratic Party and its predecessor, the CCF, made almost the same speech in the Alberta legislature. That was in the forties and fifties when Alberta was one of the "have-not" provinces and the provincial government wanted to get things going by providing a tax incentive. It was not a rip-off, it was a tax incentive.
The CCF members strongly denounced it at that time. They said it would bring ruin to the whole of the province, and so on. But that incentive created the basis for the Heritage Trust Fund which Alberta has been able to establish. It put people to work and gave them an opportunity to earn a dollar and make a profit from their industry. Today more money goes into the coffers of the government from every dollar made than goes to the oil companies which did the work. The greater profit goes to the people.
The whole story can be put in a nutshell: if you provide an incentive and do not put barnacles and shackles on free enterprise, free enterprise will produce. That is what has happened in Alberta and that is what could happen in the whole of Canada if we can get the right incentives in place. I do not consider these provisions constitute a rip-off. This is an incentive which will put people to work.
Hon. members must bear in mind that this is a high risk industry. We have to decide whether we wish to be dependent on foreign oil or whether we wish to develop our own supply. We can produce sufficient oil ourselves only if we provide incentives sufficient to induce the necessary exploration and extraction. We cannot do this with tax money because the tax burden on the population would be tremendous. It can be done, though, if we induce both small companies and large companies-and they all have their place-to go out and find the oil. Afterwards, revenues will start coming in and the people will have the advantage of the production as well as the advantage of the increased prosperity which follows that type of investment.
I have heard these prophecies of doom before from members of the party over there in that corner, and they do not make any sense to me at all. I have seen what happens when governments provide incentives. Alberta today is an example. Initiatives are still being undertaken there because the government of Alberta provides incentives. A greater amount of drilling took place in Alberta last year than that undertaken in any other place because there were better incentives, and more dollars will be made in the long run. That is exactly what can happen in Canada. We want the whole of Canada to be strong and self-sufficient so that we will not be dependent on foreign material. The free enterprise system can do it.

Mr. Chairman, when we are making a clause by clause analysis of a bill, it is essential that we deal with the bill clause by clause and not go into long harangues on philosophical subjects. We should be dealing with the clause before us. There has been diarrhoea coming from hon. members opposite.
October 31, 1979
And from your side.
It is about time we started looking at this clause and not philosophies.
What about your colleague?

This clause is to allow people not in the oil industry either as individuals or as corporations to be induced into spending their money on a most risky thing, exploration. As a result of this provision in the act, which is about to expire, all sorts of drilling funds have been organized and sold on the public market. Those drilling funds have enabled a great many more oil rigs and other things to go into the Arctic and other places. Oil and gas have been found.
This is not a long-term extension. It is a short-term extension, and it is a benefit to induce Canadians to go into a very risky enterprise. This is not a great benefit to multinational oil companies. This is not for multinational oil companies. Oil companies can already deduct their exploration expenses. They are doing it all the time. What we are attempting to do is to make this country self-sufficient in energy. What we have to do is get more private capital into the game. If that is what we are trying to do, then surely we have to approve this short-term extension. In a sense it is a benefit. It is in a sense an immediate deferral. Let us get on with it and do something to make this country self-sufficient.

Mr. Chairman, let me begin by suggesting to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine that the place to debate what party shall form the government in Manitoba is really before the people of Manitoba in Manitoba, and not here in the House of Commons. I do not mind debating the subject with the hon. member, but if he wants to know how the people of Manitoba feel I suggest to him that he look at the results of the federal election in which the members who sit here now were elected just a few months ago.
His party went into the election in Manitoba believing, and saying openly, that it was confident that it could win 12 of Manitoba's 14 seats, that the only seat it was certain it could not win was the seat occupied by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and that it was reasonably confident that it could defeat me and win all the other seats in Manitoba. The fact, of course, was that the Conservatives found themselves winning only seven of those 12 seats they expected to win on election night. Our party took five seats and the Liberals, who were supposed to be wiped out, took two seats. I say to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine that we in my party, and also the Liberals, can base our success on the kinds of policies which he and his leader in Manitoba, the Premier of Manitoba, espouse.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. We are dealing with clause 20, an amendment to the Income Tax Act, not the election results in Manitoba, the philosophy of the Manitoba government or what happened on May 22. Surely the hon. member must stay within the clause before us, or find another forum.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: 1 wish the hon. member had stood up when the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine was also a little off the clause before us. In any case, I am inviting the hon. member for Winnipeg North to come to the clause before us.

Mr. Chairman, you are, of course, correct. Had the hon. member for Mississauga South taken the same view and for the same reason called the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine to order, I would not have said the few words I have said and which I have almost concluded, namely, that if certain of us are here, it is to a large extent because of the so-called free enterprise, right-wing, do-nothing government in Manitoba. Its policy of restraint has made it so hard for senior citizens, native people, and university students in Manitoba that they rejected the Conservatives in our province and created a situation such that the federal government did not get its majority precisely because of lack of support in Manitoba.
I want to respond for a few moments to the comments made by the hon. member for Bow River. No member of my party is opposed to people, individuals, or companies in Canada getting a fair return on their investments, provided they invest their own money. What we are dealing with here, however, is not corporations or individuals who invest their own money as do investors in other industries who are content to take a reasonable profit. We are dealing here with industries, companies, and individuals who go into the field largely because they can do so without investing their own money.
I know that the hon. member for Bow River will not believe me. He will say that I am spouting socialist dogma. I suggest to the hon. member for Bow River that he read-although sometimes 1 wonder if he can or does read-a long article which ran more than a page in the Calgary Herald. I have never known the Calgary Herald to be a very radical newspaper. I do not think it has a socialist editorial policy. I do not think it is opposed to the free enterprise system, but in August it ran a long article about the activities of Dome Petroleum in the Beaufort Sea. I will not read it all, but let me read a few excerpts from the Canadian Press summary of that article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on August 24, as follows:
Canadian taxpayers may have paid as much as 93 per cent of the $150 million spent last year looking for oil in the Beaufort Sea.
But if oil is found and produced there, most of it will belong to privately-owned companies.
Despite the hundreds of millions of dollars provided in tax incentives for such northern exploration on federal lands, the federal government's share will be a fraction of the normal royalty share that Alberta gets for oil found in its jurisdiction.
And the companies investing in northern oil-using a little of their own money and a lot of the taxpayer's money-can sometimes make a profit on their investments through tax deductions, even if no oil is found.
That is one of our main complaints. We would not be objecting so strenuously if investors in oil companies were investing their own money, but they are not. What they are saying to the people of Canada is that they want tax concessions, write-offs, drilling allowances and all the rest of it. They are saying that if they do not find anything, the people of

October 31, 1979
Income Tax Act
Canada will take the loss and lose 93 cents out of every dollar invested.
"But if we get a commercial find, if we can sell the oil, if we can sell the gas, we will keep the profits. So if it is heads, we, the oil companies, win, and if it is tails, you, the people of Canada, lose."
Let us look at Dome Petroleum. Dome Petroleum was established in 1950. It is best known at present for its Beaufort Sea exploration program. It is 26 per cent owned by Dome Mines, which is in turn owned 31 per cent by Dome Pete. Dome has the distinction of never having paid a cent of income tax in its history. All its income taxes have been deferred indefinitely as a result of writing off exploration and other capital expenditures for tax purposes more rapidly than are depleted for financial accounting purposes. Although the provision for deferred income taxes shows up as liability in the company's balance sheet, its own explanation of deferred taxes is very candid. Let me quote from the 1978 annual report of the corporation as follows:
Deferred taxes appearing on the company's balance sheets do not represent a liability of the company. When Dome becomes subject to paying income taxes, it will pay tax only on the income in the year incurred, not on the income of prior years as long as the company maintains a modest level of capital expenditures.

1 rise on a point of order. The clause we are considering deals with companies which are not in the oil business and with individuals not in the oil business. Dome Petroleum is in the oil business. This member has continued to talk on matters that are not before us. He is completely off the topic. He is making a speech on what oil companies may do with their balance sheets. This is not what we are talking about here. We are talking about a special allowance for people involved in exploration which is not their normal business. How the hon. member relates anything he has said to this clause is beyond me and, I am sure, beyond anyone else in the House. He has been called to order before and I think it is essential, if we are going to get through this income tax bill, for members to talk to the particular clause in the bill before us.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Mississauga South might wish to know that what the hon. member for Winnipeg North was referring to with regard to Dome Petroleum is exactly what is in the clause, because Dome Petroleum is a company engaging in explorations in the Beaufort Sea which has attracted private companies and individuals not in the oil industry to make investments, and is using these funds to generate tax write-offs for the individuals who have bought shares in these funds. So in fact the hon. member for Winnipeg North is right on target in his remarks.

Mr. Chairman, let me just say with regard to the point which the hon. member for Mississauga South raised that, although I do not like to be personal, I am much more to the point on this subject than the hon. member has been in his frequent letters to the newspapers about matters such as the native people, about whom he knows less than nothing.
(Mr. Orlikow.]
Let me continue to quote from the 1976 annual report of Dome Petroleum. It reads as follows:
Provided the company maintains a modest oil and gas exploration and capital investment program, it is unlikely that the accumulated deferred income taxes will become payable.
As the hon. member who spoke a couple of minutes ago pointed out, that is exactly why we are concerned, because Dome is doing what so many other companies in this field have done. They are attracting capital by telling people, quite properly under our regulations, that they can get a much better net return after they pay taxes if they invest in this form of activity rather than in others. At the end of 1978, Dome's deferred taxes totalled $209 million, which was an increase of 436 per cent or $170 million since the end of 1973. In other words, between 1974 and 1978, Dome accumulated 81 per cent of its deferred taxes as a result of the federal government's tax policy largesse.
There are only a few minutes left before five o'clock, Mr. Chairman-
We are going on to six o'clock.

It has been pointed out to me that we are going on to six o'clock, Mr. Chairman, so I have a few more moments.
I will conclude by saying to the parliamentary secretary that when one looks at how we treated the oil and gas companies, at how we have encouraged investment in these fields-nobody questioned the need to look for oil and gas and other energy sources which may be available in Canada-and when one looks at the real rate of taxation which individuals or corporations investing in these fields pay, and how low that tax rate is compared to the tax rate paid by people who invest in the manufacturing industry, and when you consider the fact that over the last ten or 15 years Canada has had the highest rate of increase in the labour force of any of the western industrialized countries, and when you realize that while manufacturing, which is labour intensive, pays a high rate of taxation- something over 40 per cent-and that our resource industries, which are capital intensive and which employ relatively few people, pay a very low rate of taxation, it is no wonder that Canadian and foreign funds flow into the resource industry rather than into the manufacturing industry.
What the government is proposing in this clause is a further concession, a further inducement to people to invest in this field because they will pay less taxes than in other fields and therefore their real return will be higher than in other fields. The government is doing that precisely at a time when we should be doing the exact reverse, precisely at a time when we should be marshalling all our forces, putting all our efforts into encouraging the manufacturing industry, which is declining from year to year.
Our share of the Canadian market and of the international market has been dropping, and the number of people, the percentage of the Canadian work force, employed in the manufacturing industry has declined from 26 per cent a few years ago to just under 20 per cent at present. So what we
October 31, 1979

should have are measures to encourage the manufacturing industry. What we should have are research and development incentives, and programs to get our industries working. What we should have is concentration on developing our manufacturing industries. Instead, what we are getting from this Conservative government is just more of what we got from the former Liberal government, more concessions to the resource industry, more encouragement to go into the oil and gas field at no risk to the investor but at a great loss to the people of Canada. The loss is in the form of taxes which we forgo, in the form of higher prices which we pay, and all that at a time when we should be concentrating our efforts on getting people to work in those fields which in every other country employ 25 per cent or more of the labour force, and which we are ignoring almost completely.

Mr. Chairman, may I be permitted to speak very briefly on this subject which has been well covered this afternoon. A few days ago we were treated to the spectacle of the hon. member for Oshawa telling us of his concern for the Toronto stock exchange. Today the hon. member for Broad-view-Greenwood told us of his concern about interference in the free market, in this case the free market for capital, it seems at long last they are learning something over on that side.
I should like to elaborate a little on what was said by the parliamentary secretary concerning the fact that this legislation is designed to get away from the concentration which exists in the oil industry. This legislation gives an opportunity to ordinary people like members of the House of Commons. Should an hon. member wish to invest and take advantage of the provisions of the income tax bill before us, he will be able to use his capital in order to reduce the amount of concentration which exists in these industries.
A policy of energy self-sufficiency must be adopted in Canada. This is one of the elements of such a policy. It is much better if we can work toward energy self-sufficiency through private investment rather than through organizations such as Petro-Canada which are so heavily dependent upon government support. This is the correct type of legislation through which to encourage private investment. It has been on the books for some time. If one goes to Calgary or another exploration centre in Canada, one will find out that it is working successfully. It is attracting money from Canadians in all walks of life. It has proven to be successful. As a result of this type of incentive, a lot of oil and gas and a considerable amount of minerals have been found in the country. It is legislation like this that enables and will enable all Canadians to get in on the energy boom which could hit us at any time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask a brief question before getting into my main remarks. The parliamentary secretary suggested that this is another tax deferral. Before entering into a discussion on that, 1 should like to know what is the amount of tax deferral owed to Canadians now? If we are to make a judgment on whether it is desirable to
Income Tax Act
continue or elaborate on this, will the parliamentary secretary tell us what is the present amount of deferred taxes owed to Canadians?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I will see if there is such a figure available, but 1 would quarrel with the words of the hon. member. So-called deferred tax is not owed to the government until income is earned, if an enterprise is not successful, that can be never. It is a very simple situation. One incurs expenses to be in a business, and one is allowed to charge them against other income not earned in the particular project for which the expenses are incurred. One will never owe tax on that project unless one subsequently earns income.
It is not owed to the government in any sense. I am not sure if there is a statistical figure available for the sum total of what are called deferred taxes by the accounting profession. It is a phrase which I have never thought was very illuminating. In fact I think it is misleading.
Try $100 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should think that would be small. The best 1 can do at this moment is to repeat that this particular measure is estimated to defer taxes at the rate of $80 million a year. Whether there is a figure for all deferred taxes which go far beyond the oil industry, I am not sure. It is called deferred taxes if you write off depreciation in the manufacturing business, for instance, faster than the normal life of the asset. I think such a figure might be very hard to achieve. It may exist, but I am not sure.

Mr. Chairman, I have a supplementary question. When the government produces its tax expenditure figures, is it the intention of the government to give us the total cost of capital cost allowance deferrals? Will that figure be included in the accounting?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am afraid I cannot give the hon. member an answer on that because 1 just do not happen to know it. Personally 1 have some reservations about this tax expenditure concept. It seems to be based on the idea that somehow or other all revenue belongs to the government and any reduction from that is a tax expenditure. In any event we are committed to giving some information at the time of the budget on what have come to be called tax expenditures. I am not sure whether it will cover deferred taxation or not. I am not sure if I could find out that information in advance of the budget.

Supplementary to that, I should like to indicate to the parliamentary secretary that he and I may disagree on the usefulness of the concept of tax expenditure. 1 assume from what the Minister of Finance has told us that he and the President of the Treasury Board have accepted the notion. I hope it will be included. If he cannot give us the figure requested by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River, perhaps he could tell us the total cost of section 66 of the Income Tax Act? Can he give us that figure, which includes oil companies, prospectors and other groups?
