Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am informed that there is no such estimate available at the moment. It is possible it may be included in the budget figures which will be submitted. I will make a note of it and suggest it to the minister.

The matter which bothers me, as I mentioned the other day, is that the tax system is a very difficult and imprecise method of governing the economy. When a tax saving is provided to people in one particular sector, we deprive others. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North said, we wind up literally forcing individual taxpayers to fund this program.
Also I am concerned with the statements of the hon. member for Bow River when he suggested that incentives created the great wealth in Alberta. It appears to me that that is not logical. The real boom in Alberta, and the program which developed therefrom, evolved more at the hands of the Ayatollah than anything done in Alberta. There are certain directions in Alberta today which will be very helpful in the future. 1 am referring to the attempt to diversify the basic economy of Alberta.
Rather than putting forward provisions such as this, perhaps we should look at using other instruments to direct the investments of this country into some of our other resource bases. We should not place this country into a resource dependent position. We should try to capitalize on some of our resource bases. If Alberta is successful in diversifying its industry, when that resource is depleted, surely we will see a much stronger province than the one which existed before the group led by the Ayatollah put Alberta in such a favourable position. In my opinion it has little to do with incentives. The fact is that the oil, gas and coal were in the ground when the dinosaurs roamed.
You mean when the Social Credit party was in power.

Hold it, please. Let me continue. You will have lots of time in a moment. There has been a suggestion that it was incentives such as this that helped to improve Alberta, incentives similar to the one in the act as described by the parliamentary secretary.
Let me refer to one other fact, and that is that as a result of incentives like this, or otherwise, we have now developed or found more gas than we can use. This is the result of incentives for investments such as this. That gas is now capped, and we find people before the National Energy Board attempting to export that gas across the border. This is what the taxpayers' money has done. What we have essentially done is produce an energy source we cannot use, and in fact we are now going to give the benefit of that to another country.
The suggestion is that perhaps we should, through incentives of various types, or by some mechanism, direct this investment into other industries so that we can increase employment in this country, maybe offsetting some of the problems we have as a result of importing high cost goods. Another implication

was that we should be encouraging individuals and small businesses to get into the oil business. That is almost an impossible hope, particularly in view of the way we are attempting to do that. The oil business is clearly controlled and held by the seven sisters, and to suggest anything else would be foolish.
We see on the one hand investments by small businesses and individuals being encouraged, while on the other hand they are being strangled by the fact that in order to borrow capital to make some of these investments they must pay prohibitive interest rates. Interest rates are in turn driven up and borrowing becomes even more difficult. We have contradictory efforts being made here. The one put forward in this clause should be the most appropriate one, and there should not be other government programs in direct contradiction to it.
Those are some of the things that concern me, and perhaps the parliamentary secretary can provide the answers. I am basically asking what industrial strategy affecting the total economy underpins the decision to adopt these tax savings for resource companies and other people who are encouraged to get into the resource business? What is being aimed at in the over-all picture?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to comment on some of the remarks and implications by the hon. member, and also by the hon. member for Winnipeg North. It seems difficult to me to comprehend how, at a time when the whole world is energy short and Canada has the potential to be self-sufficient in energy, a situation which would be of great benefit to the economy of this country, one could question any reasonable effort to induce expenditure on exploration for the development of our energy potential. I might point out that when such expenditures are made they do not disappear into nothingness. Those expenditures in many cases are for manufactured products. The steel industry of Saskatchewan and the steel industry of Ontario are two of the areas to which that money goes. The food industry and all of the industries that supply drilling equipment, which involve a difficult logistics exercise, all share in these expenditures.
Surely it is clear that this country needs energy, that it has the potential for self-sufficiency in energy, but that will not be realized if investment is not induced, and it will not be induced if it is not attractive.
I had the privilege of seeing the oil exploration industry in this country grow from practically zero in 1947 to a very substantial industry of very great strength to the economy of this country. The industry was not built by the Ayatollah, it was built by sensible government policies that encouraged what proved to be, on balance, along with a lot of losing investments, a substantial success in discovering oil and gas reserves in this country.
It so happens that exploration success in this business, as in mining, tends to occur in jumps. You can go along for years, spend, spend, find nothing and become discouraged. Then you may have a brief period of great success. The policies followed in this country have produced gas which at the moment is
October 31, 1979

surplus to our current needs. That is an asset which we should not deplore or question. We should congratulate ourselves. This is an asset whether we keep it in the ground, or follow the suggestion that we export some of that gas.
The hon. member talked about interest rates and asked why we have high interest rates in this country. One very powerful reason is that we are borrowing to keep alive. We are borrowing at the rate of $7 billion to $8 billion in the current year. If that were not the case and we were not under that kind of debtor's burden, we would not necessarily require these high interest rates. That natural gas surplus could help us earn our way in the world a bit better. It could contribute to ameliorating the conditions that have caused present high interest rates.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North spoke of things about which 1 am very sympathetic. He spoke of the need in this country for a more competitive, successful and dynamic manufacturing sector. He pointed to the way in which it has declined. I agree that we need to do something about the lack of dynamism in the manufacturing sector, or a large part of it in this country. We need this for purposes of employment and we need it to help pay our way in the world.
We also need this measure which is directed to something equally as important: self-sufficiency in energy in this country for the next several decades. These two needs are not competitive. In fact, as 1 mentioned a few moments earlier, the manufacturing sector can be helped through exploration and development expenditures, and by investment in pipelines and all of those things that come with success.
While I share some of the concerns of the hon. member, they really have nothing to do with taking a negative attitude toward this particular provision. 1 might also point out that this particular provision has nothing to do with some of the claims that have been made that investors can get something for nothing through tax revenues in this country. This provision is simply concerned with writing off legitimate exploration expenses. Depending on one's tax rate, which can scarcely be higher in this country than something like 62 per cent, that is all it can save you. It cannot save you 110 per cent. The hon. member is talking about something different when he is talking about that. He is talking about what is called superdepletion. That is something that is not being debated at this point. That is a debate which I suppose depends on what comes out in the budget.
This clause is not doing some of the things that remarks from the other side would suggest. It will make a substantial contribution to the promotion of self-sufficiency in energy in this country, and I can think of nothing more important for at least the next two decades.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to respond to some of the things said by the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, the hon. member for Mississauga South, the hon. member for the Western Arctic and others. We seem to have managed to stir some of the true believers in the Conservative party out of their doldrums.
Income Tax Act
First of all, there is the question of relevance. This clause is an amendment to section 66 of the Income Tax Act. That section deals with the question of Canadian exploration and development expenses, and the way in which those expenses are written off. With due respect to the hon. member for Mississauga South, we are entitled, in view of that amendment, to talk about section 66, its effects, and the importance and relationship of this deduction to other deductions and, therefore, entitled to take this opportunity to ask the government to look at what is happening to our tax system, how fair it is, how effective it is, and whether it is achieving the results which we wanted it to achieve.
The member for Mississauga South reminds me of the person who was asked in an examination, "what is Moby Dick about?", and his answer was, "Moby Dick is about a whale". That is not a very imaginative or complete answer, because Moby Dick is about many things. It is about life itself. This section of the Income Tax Act is not just about the whale that is contained in clause 20, it is about the whole section 66 which deals with the very important feature of the tax system in Canada, and a very important innovation which was brought in by the Liberal party and to which my party has taken exception. We are using this as an opportunity to ask the government to look at that section again, and I think that we are perfectly entitled to do that because that is what Parliament is all about.
As for the intervention by the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine with his usual deftness, subtlety, and his concern for accuracy and fairness, I thought that he was going to talk about Shell Oil and Dome Petroleum, because the last time I spoke in this House he took such exception to my remarks he said that I was misleading the House and that he would come back and correct all the misleading information I had given to the House so that the truth would be known, because all that came forth from this party was untruth and error of fact and in interpretation.
Of course, the reason that the hon. member could not come into the House and correct the error and the untruth I was speaking is because the facts I was telling this House are correct. The interpretation of course is philosophical, and members of this House are entitled to take exception to that, but I see no reason to be abusive in taking exception to that philosophy. I happen to think that the philosophy and points of view which the member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine espouses have a disastrous effect on working people. It is terribly unfair, and it can be a vicious attack on the standard of living of the average Canadian.
The hon. member thinks that the two effects of the policies we follow are to drive business to bankruptcy and out of the country and to destroy what he refers to as the productive sector of the economy. With due respect to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, these discussions have been going on in industrial society since it was created. I do not see any reason for being particularly abusive about it. It is simply a difference of approach and interest, and I will leave the matter at that. We are certainly entitled to that difference without the

October 31, 1979
Income Tax Act
kind of abuse and general derision that we always get from the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine.
The parliamentary secretary, 1 believe, said two basic things in answer to my original intervention. The first thing was that one judges the worth-while nature of a tax incentive by its success, and that if a tax incentive managed to achieve what it was designed to achieve, then it was successful. That suggestion in itself is very limited and one-dimensional.
In the early 1970s, there was a virtual strike of capital because of what the multinational oil companies felt was an unfair system of taxation in Canada. They refused to invest in frontier exploration and drilling. In some circles that would be known as a form of bargaining, that is, using their bargaining power by withdrawing their capital and refusing to invest. In other circles it would be known as economic blackmail. Members of the party opposite have taken the same view when they talk about a strike of labour. Some people refer to a strike as collective bargaining, while some extremists on the other side, such as the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, would no doubt regard a strike as a form of blackmail.
Faced with that strike on the part of capital, the Canadian government had two choices. It could either knuckle under and give the industry what it wanted, or it could take the industry over. It could move toward public ownership. In the case of the Liberal government, and because it was a Liberal government, it did neither and it did both at the same time. It moved toward partial public ownership in the sense that it created Petro-Canada, but, of course, it did not give Petro-Canada the power that it needed. There was no public ownership or nationalization of Imperial Oil, Gulf, Shell or any of the other oil companies. The other thing which the Liberal party did was to provide this extraordinary range of incentives.
What the parliamentary secretary is telling us is, "Look, we have a problem. The problem is that we need to develop our oil and gas supplies. We have a bunch of multinational companies which are engaged in that business. How do we get them to do that business? We give them an incentive. If the incentive is sufficient and they are out developing the oil and gas, it therefore is working and is worth the price."
I suggest that this theory ignores some very important questions such as what is the price of the incentive, who pays the price of the incentive, who reaps the benefit of the incentive, and what kind of economic system functions like this? 1 am afraid that the parliamentary secretary cannot answer these questions. 1 honestly do not think that the Conservative party, with its philosophy and its commitment to this economic system under which we are now living, is able to deal with that problem.
Large multinational companies have gained control of the resources and are coming to the government and saying, "Look, this is the price of development". The Conservative party, with all respect to the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, has as one of its major platforms and has indicated in all its public statements since the election and in the creation of the task force on Petro-Canada, that it is getting rid of Petro-Canada, that it is selling it off to the private

sector, and that the exploration and development parts will be sold to the private sector.
We do not know exactly what their plans are, but the plan in the task force report would permit the control of Petro-Canada by a group of large multinational companies with Canadian subsidiaries. If each one of those groups owned 2 per cent of the shares, five of them would own 10 per cent of these shares, and there is not any economist in Canada who would not say that if one owns 10 per cent of the shares of a large corporation one is able to control the direction of that corporation, because the rest of the shares would be sufficiently diversified that no one else would have control.
With respect to the first answer that the parliamentary secretary gave us, which was the answer of the Conservative party and the Liberal party before it, that since this is accomplishing what it was set out to accomplish, the answer is yes, the question which I was raising, and with respect I do not think the hon. member can answer it because it goes beyond the terms of reference of his party was: is it worth the price? What are the alternatives? The alternatives are philosophically unacceptable to the Conservative party, but I suggest that they are cheaper in the long run to the Canadian people and will guarantee that the benefits of research, development and exploration in oil will stay in Canada and be controlled by Canadians.
At what price do we continue to subsidize multinational and corporate development? It is like the case of Ford or General Motors deciding whether or not to go into Quebec. It is like the case of all these incentives and grants that are being talked about, whether directly or indirectly. The nature of our economic system is changing, and those true believers on the other side who do not recognize it will wake up with a shock one day.
The second question was the manufacturing one. With great respect to the parliamentary secretary, I do not think it is far-fetched to say that there are other reasons for our lack of competitiveness. The hon. member stressed the wages question, but I would stress lack of investment along with some of the structural weaknesses of Canadian industry. We cannot make much progress when we have a branch plant economy. It is impossible for that economy to expand and grow and concentrate unless there is planning and direction co-ordinated for the public good. That is the main problem, not the problem of wages, the one the hon. member brought up.
I say to the parliamentary secretary that it is not far-fetched to suggest-and this theory is not unique to me-that where you have a tax system that gives extraordinary benefits and an exceptionally low level of tax to the oil and gas industry, and where similar benefits are not given to the manufacturing sector, there will be distortions of capital investment. That is exactly what is happening.
The hon. member for Western Arctic in his intervention drew attention to himself for the second time since I have been here. The first time he had a teddy bear on his desk. The second time, in his child-like faith, he expressed the rights of
October 31, 1979

multinational oil companies to continue to develop Canadian resources willy-nilly. In my opinion this is no longer adequate. We are looking at a set-up which is giving tremendous benefits through our tax system. Eventually the Canadian people will want to know what the cost is. The cost that I have suggested-1 think I am right but only time will tell, although 1 hope my predictions will prove wrong-will be a continued weakness in the manufacturing sector and there will be a total takeover and domination of our resource sector.
These things need to be said. Members on the other side want this to go through without any debate-I know it is in the interest of the Liberal party for it go through because it is embarrassed, it knows the measures and what they contain. The Liberals know they cannot defend them. They know they are not an opposition party but a government in exile. They never accepted the fact that they lost the election on May 22, and that they have no real basis either in philosophy, economics or politics on which to oppose this budget and these tax measures. I suggest the phantom opposition has disappeared and that the main opposition falls to members of this party. We are happy to fill that role. We intend to fill the role. We do not intend to disappear or make things easy for the government just because this is not its budget. It is a budget of "tight money's" first team instead of "tight money's" second team. We are glad to oppose it.

Mr. Chairman, I will speak briefly. We have heard some profound statements on where we are. As politicians, one of the reasons we disagree is that we do not share the same set of assumptions at all. We are arguing usually from a different base. It does not mean that all the righteous are over here. Sometimes we are told that only the self-righteous are over here and all the "Evel Knievels" are sitting opposite. 1 would withdraw the word "all", but certainly there are some we could disagree with.
We are not opposed to development nor to self sufficiency nor incentives. What we are concerned about is the nature of the development and the nature of the incentives. One of my colleagues mentioned, following the address by the hon. member for Bow River, that one of our problems is with the manufacturing industry, and that if we could develop a manufacturing industry from our indigenous resources, that would be all to the good of the country. We have not seen that happen. Quite the reverse, except in the case of Alberta.
The Ayatollah did not put the oil in the ground in Alberta; neither did Peter Lougheed nor Premier Manning who spent his life damning the banks as a Social Creditor and then joined the board of one of them. It is an accident, and some of us have been told that in spite of all its oil and gas, because it lacks entrepreneurial skills Alberta was once in receivership. It has not always been an affluent place. We are not opposed to incentives. If this clause was intended to give incentives to companies, whether spin-off companies of the multinationals or not, we would prefer them to be Canadian-owned, to provide secondary and tertiary manufacturing as is being discussed. I think that is the aim of Alberta's Heritage Fund. So if we listen to the "fast buck" artists who are so anxious to
Income Tax Act
save us from our balance of payment deficit and ship all the cheap gas and oil across the border as soon as possible, I think Peter Lougheed has a right to be piling up all those royalties in his Heritage Fund. In a short while Alberta will need these funds for diversification. You can provide all the incentives you like but if there is no oil in the ground, that is it.
A number of people I have talked to are saying we ought not to believe there is a shortage. They are saying these bloody oil companies have some oil, and what they are doing is capping it until the price goes up. The parliamentary secretary has tried to clarify this for us. Under this clause we are not talking about capital cost allowances or fancy write-offs or anything, but that is irrelevant to our position in explaining the assumptions we are dealing with. It is not that we are opposed to the use of incentives per se. What we are saying is that we are not interested in being blackmailed or bribed or in providing bribes to companies that are doing very well in terms of their own profitability.
I am reminded that the premier of Newfoundland, Brian Peckford, has had some experience with oil companies. He has decided to deal with resource companies on his own terms. There was a strike, but in two years the workers were back on his terms. I suggest that we can do all the bribery we want and justify it in any way we like, but the oil companies are in the business of digging up oil and the mining companies are in the business of digging up minerals. If they are not able to do that they will not function very long as mining companies. It is not to anyone's advantage to see them disappear. What we are questioning is the need for these new incentives. At two dollars a barrel, companies were exploring all over the place, yet that was the time the major strikes occurred. The parliamentary secretary is more acquainted with the oil companies than we on this side, perhaps, but he can correct me if I am wrong.
The hon. member for Western Arctic thought these writeoffs in terms of exploration would contribute to a massive development of people's capital in this country. I would like to remind him that fewer than 10 per cent of Canadians, mainly the affluent, own any stocks at all. While we are willing to give tax breaks to the resource companies and oil companies, despite the promise of a $2 billion tax cut for low and middle-income Canadians during the last campaign we are now told by the Minister of Finance we cannot afford it. We can afford to give these tax breaks though.
One of the justifications used by the parliamentary secretary is that tax breaks do not disappear into nothing. After they are spent by companies, and they are going to be spent unless they are used as profits, banked or shipped out of the country to be invested in foreign lands, they are spent on various things that contribute to our economy. By giving these companies these breaks we do benefit and get back our taxes in other ways. There is a good deal of logic in that.
Could the same point not be made for any kind of subsidy? For example, could it not be made by a small businessman in a Newfoundland, Ontario or British Columbia town who is on

October 31, 1979
Income Tax Act
U1C? After all, UIC funds are spent in the local community. Any kind of subsidy can be justified that way, even welfare or old age pensions.
Yesterday we were told that we cannot afford $9 billion to up the old age pension to the poverty line. However, we have a proposal which will cost precisely that, maybe not the same, but it is a similar fund for another purpose.
The parliamentary secretary, not deliberately, indulges in a bit of sophistry when he tells us that money given to any one group of people, such as resource companies, is stimulating the economy and is not going down the tube. It is not lost into nothing. However, he conveniently ignores the other forms of transfer payments of wealth which do precisely the same thing. That is a particularly important point.
There is one small item to which I wish to speak. I do not know whether the parliamentary secretary's former company has anything to do with any of the gas distributing companies that are so anxious to sell off our gas to the United States in return for lowering our balance of exchange deficit of between $7 and $9 billion a year. According to the figures I have, 13 per cent of our budget is used precisely for that purpose. I do not think anyone on this side disagrees that this is a very serious matter. Whether we can do much about it through methods such as this or selling off our cheap and accessible resources, as we have done with our oil which will force us into frontier expensive oil at tremendous risk in terms of the environment, is precisely another question. I put that before you, not because I have any final answer but merely because it is a question of concern to many Canadians. We do not necessarily think that decisions based on the profit motive, avarice, greed or whatever you want to call it, always add up to the best interests of our nation. That is where we part company with those who sit over there and with some of those who sit here.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add a few comments in response to what the parliamentary secretary has said. They have been fairly well developed by the other two members who have spoken. I am concerned about the proposition that this kind of amendment to the Income Tax Act will create a situation where we will have more gas to export and therefore the exporting of that gas and other resources will provide us with a mechanism to offset the deficit in our balance of payments. That kind of logic occurred several years ago.
1 have a vague recollection of oil companies in this country suggesting there was not enough oil and that in fact we were running out. The price escalated and a lot of fright covered the land. Shortly after that the price rose. All of a sudden we were told they had underestimated the reserves and that we were in a position to export. The executives of the oil companies in this country suggested that we should start to pump the gas and oil over our borders and derive the benefit of this very vital thing that was surplus to our needs at that time.
Again today we are short. We do not have enough. We will run out in the eighties unless we make tremendous investment in the offshore expensive frontier areas. The question you have

to ask, and this is the problem in this clause, and the whole section we are dealing with, is why has no energy policy been stated by this government? We talk about self-sufficiency, but no clear direction has been set down that we can support. Leadership in the energy policy area has been put out by the energy companies. They are the ones suggesting we should be saving ourselves from a situation that sees us with a terrible balance of payments, a declining dollar, high priced imports, unemployment, and failure to diversify our industry.
I realize the benefits that accrue from that. Essentially we are back to the same old question, what is the direction? When are we going to hear from the government a clear policy direction that will justify putting in this or any other clause? What we are doing is putting in the mechanism and then developing the rationale for it.
This particular type of thing may or may not generate more oil and gas, and may or may not result in more individuals freeing up capital. Capital in this country is very scarce. What we need is a sense of direction as to where it will be invested. The people of this country should know this. Obviously Exxon, Gulf, Royal Dutch Shell and some other companies in this country do not have our goals at heart. Theirs is profit. Somehow it is expected the two will link together, our needs and theirs. That certainly has not proven to be the case in the past.
The area served by the hon. member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands, and my area of Comox-Powell River, are very short of energy. The kind of clause suggested here will not help us a lot unless we do not export to the United States, but ship to Vancouver Island and along the coast of British Columbia where we are energy short. We now buy energy at an extremely high rate.
We developed a cable to Vancouver Island that at one point was estimated would cost every family on the island $4,000 and there would be a continuous high price for electricity. If we are to have an energy self-sufficient policy, we must look at a variety of forms and not just extremely expensive investment.
Something else that concerns me has been stated before and is worth stating again. When you give benefits to a very small segment of the Canadian population, you provide those benefits at the expense of a lot of other people who are not so well off on the income scale. It strikes me that when people put up surplus capital and they obtain tax benefits like this, not just the profit behind it, others are in fact paying. I wonder what benefit a lot of people along the coast of British Columbia who earn modest incomes will derive from exporting gas to the United States and exporting coal to Japan when we are not providing diversity in industry, and not providing energy to places like Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands in an efficient form.
I want to come to the business of interest rates, the devalued dollar and our balance of payments. The B.C. Hydro Corporation went to New York to borrow billions upon billions to deliver energy in a form that is not necessarily the most efficient. The federal government has no suggestion on how we might provide these things in a very efficient pattern to areas
October 31, 1979

of the country that need them. Heavy concentration on high-cost areas is not what we need. Capital is scarce. We need to channel it in areas of investment which are extremely important. If this kind of tax amendments results in our exporting gas, it is not what we should be doing.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I have given notice to the Minister of Finance that we intend to discuss the small business tax changes in the course of this debate. Could the parliamentary secretary tell us what he considers to be the appropriate clause on which to discuss the changes in the small business tax rate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
1 think clause 38 would be the best one.
Clauses 24 to 31 inclusive agreed to.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, I ask you to slow down. You are reading the numbers of clauses faster than we can find out what an individual clause is about.
Clauses 32 to 37 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 38-

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. We indicated on second reading and I have indicated to the minister, that we are not happy about this particular change. There are two aspects on which I should like to hear explanations from the parliamentary secretary. Anyone who has had the misfortune to become involved with the Income Tax Act knows that the complexity of adding a third type of corporation creates an unnecessary anomaly and adds to the existing confusion. We started out with a purpose in according a particular rate, a 25 per cent rate, to small businesses earning between $150,000 and $750,000. There was a purpose behind that provision. It was to bring taxation relief to companies which were providing employment and expanding their operations in a very important sector of the economy. It is worth noting that the vast majority of Canadian workers are employed in small business. I see that the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Industry is here this afternoon, shaking his head whenever I get up, and I am sure he will have some comments to make about the positions which have been taken.
We can understand the purpose behind that differentiation in the rate but under the amendment a variety of people- journalists, hockey players, actors, doctors, lawyers, chartered accountants-are taking advantage of the small business cor-
Income Tax Act
poration provision to incorporate themselves and reduce their effective rate of taxation. I am sorry the hon. member for Saint-Henri-Westmount is not here because I know that though he disagrees with me on many things he would agree with me on this one.
The fiction of becoming a corporation is not readily understood by the average citizen. The average citizen does not earn enough money to concern himself with whether he should be paying the private rate or the small business corporate rate or the large business corporate rate, or whatever. The vast majority of Canadians get their cheques, income tax is paid at source, they are entitled to certain deductions, and that is all there is to it. There are no capital cost allowances or capital gains or any of the other complexities of the act to be considered. For 90 per cent of the taxpayers of Canada the income tax legislation is simple-they pay their money and they get very little by way of deductions. It only becomes complicated when a taxpayer has a lot of money.
One of the anomalies I should like the parliamentary secretary to explain is this: why has the decision been made to create this third category in addition to the other two, the standard corporate rate and the small business rate? It will be difficult to establish who fits into this new category. It makes no sense from the point of view of stimulating the economy. These are not people who generate a lot of business opportunities. The amendment is simply a mechanism for allowing certain groups, mainly professionals, the advantages of corporations so that they can pay a lower rate of income tax.
I should like to hear an explanation of what the Minister of Finance meant in his statement accompanying the change when he said this would have a tax-neutral effect. I should like the parliamentary secretary to explain how that can be the case. I think I know what he means. It is not tax neutral between what he would have been paying as a private citizen, it is another form of tax neutrality, but I think it is misleading for the minister to say that this will be tax-neutral because it certainly is not; it is a reduction in the effective rate of taxation of upper middle income people. It is important to understand what is happening. It is increasing it from now, but it is reducing it from what it would be if we disallowed the incorporation provision.

Progress reported.
